records.name_note: NC State's dedicated Alternanthera ficoidea page is the only admissible dedicated page retrieved. Its rendered H1 is the bare binomial, and its rendered Common Name(s) list is alphabetized: Bloodleaf, Calico Plant, Copperleaf, Joseph's Coat, Joyweed, Parrot Leaf, with Bloodleaf first. Its Description prose calls the plant 'Joseph's coat', a name this catalog already uses for Amaranthus tricolor, so the record leads with the list's first item, Bloodleaf. No admissible page was retrieved for A. dentata or A. bettzickiana, so nothing is asserted about how they relate to this name.
unknowns: Only one admissible dedicated page was readable: NC State's Alternanthera ficoidea page. MoBot's page (taxonid=275668) could not be fetched; plantfinder.mobot.org failed with ConnectError after retries, and curl hit an SSL certificate verification error on that host.

RHS has no retrievable dedicated page for the species (the plants/alternanthera-ficoidea URL returned 404); the only RHS hit was for the cultivar 'Snowball', which is not species evidence. No UF/IFAS or Clemson species page was found; the UF/IFAS Alternanthera page found was for A. maritima, a different species.

NC State's page has no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags, so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null (no record, not a safety finding). It does not address eating, so is_edible is null.
NC State has no Attracts field, so attracts_pollinators is null.
soil_base is null. NC State gives 'High Organic Matter' and good drainage, which does not map cleanly to one enum token for a plant grown both in beds and in containers.

water_regime is null. The only moisture language is the soil adjective 'moist' and the '#moist soil' tag, not a watering statement; the Soil Drainage tags list 'Occasionally Wet' alongside 'Good Drainage'.
NC State's Life Cycle field lists both Annual and Perennial, and USDA zones 10a-11b.

Light tags also list 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)'; no species-specific direct-sun-hours figure is given, so direct_sun_hours_max is null. The prose notes leaves may bleach in full sun during hot summers.

Sibling A. dentata (also sold as calico plant) was not researched here and must not be merged with this record. 'Joseph's Coat' is shared with the landed Amaranthus tricolor, a different species, though no admissible page was cited for that contrast.

common_name researched as 'Calico Plant' (the batch request); landed as 'Bloodleaf', the first item of NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list, because Calico Plant is only its second item and the Description's prose lead, "Joseph's coat", is already Amaranthus tricolor's landed name.

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated page leads with Sea Lavender (first item of its alphabetized Common Name(s) list: Sea Lavender, Statice, Wavyleaf Sea Lavender), and its description prose calls the plant Statice. RHS's profile leads with purple-cup't statice (Other common names: purple-cup't statice, thrift). Both Sea Lavender and Statice are also used by NC State for other species, so neither name is unique to L. sinuatum. The record lands as Statice, the name NC State's Description opens with ('Statice is a short lived, summer flowering, herbaceous perennial ...'); Sea Lavender is the alternative.

toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail and is_edible are null: the NC State page for this species has no Poison, Problem-for-Cats/Dogs or edibility field and no admissible source addresses them.

soil_drainage left null: NC State lists 'Good Drainage' with 'Occasionally Dry' and the prose says 'dry to medium moisture, well-drained', which is not an explicit sharp-drainage statement (so not fast) and not the Good Drainage + Moist pair (so not moderate).
soil_ph left null: NC State ticks Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0) and Alkaline (>8.0), and the open-ended bands give no bound.
water_regime left null: NC State says 'Do not over-water to prevent root and crown rot' and 'dry to medium moisture', which does not map cleanly to one regime token. No watering interval is stated.
soil_base left null: NC State describes in-ground sandy loams and also lists Container as a landscape location, so no single base token is supported.
NC State says 'Plants will sometimes struggle in high heat or humidity'; this is not a humidity requirement, so humidity fields are null.

NC State lists Life Cycle Annual, Biennial and Perennial, and Plant Type as Herbaceous Perennial. It describes the plant as short lived and not particularly hardy, grown as an annual in zones higher than 8 or as a biennial, so temperature fields are null.
No fertilizing guidance in the admissible pages found, so the fertilizer fields are null.

records.name_note: Only one admissible source with a dedicated page for this exact name could be read (NC State). Its Common Name(s) list is alphabetized: African Rosemallow, Cranberry Hibiscus, False Roselle, Maroon Mallow, Red Hibiscus, Red-leaved Hibiscus. The first list entry is therefore African Rosemallow, but the Description prose opens with 'Cranberry hibiscus', so that lead name is used. NC State also lists 'Previously known as: Hibiscus eetveldeanus'.
unknowns: Only NC State Plant Toolbox (plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/hibiscus-acetosella/) was readable as a dedicated page for this exact name. Missouri Botanical Garden / plantfinder.mobot.org could not be fetched (connection errors, host refuses non-browser clients). No RHS page for Hibiscus acetosella was found (guessed URL 404; search page is script-rendered). No UF/IFAS (edis/ask) page for this species was found. Clemson HGIC mentions it only on a multi-species Hibiscus factsheet, which was not used as a dedicated page.

Toxicity: the NC State page has no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags, and no other admissible source was read, so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null (no record, not a finding of safety).

Edibility: the NC State page does not address eating at all (the leaves are eaten as a sour green in the tropics per general knowledge, but no admissible source read states it), so is_edible is null. The ornamental cultivars listed (e.g. 'Mahogony Splendor', 'Red Shield') imply nothing about edibility. NC State lists 'False Roselle' as an alias; this is not Hibiscus sabdariffa (roselle).

Water: NC State gives only soil adjectives ('average to moist but not wet soil'; Soil Drainage tags Good Drainage and Moist), not a watering statement, so water_regime and all watering interval fields are null.

Frost: NC State says 'sometimes plants die from frost before flowers appear' and lists USDA zones 9a-11b, but gives no damage-onset temperature, so chill_damage_f is null. It is also described as 'a tender perennial sub-shrub' that may not survive year-round outdoors and can be overwintered as a houseplant.

Soil mix (soil_base), pH, humidity, light in foot-candles, temperature ranges, fertilizing and direct-sun hours max are not stated on the NC State page and are left null. NC State's Light tag is Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day), which is the site-wide category label, not a species maximum.
Pollinators: NC State's Wildlife Value sentence is genus-level (Members of the genus Hibiscus); attracts_pollinators rests on the species page's Attracts field (Bees, Specialized Bees) and bee tags.

records.name_note: The catalog brief calls this plant Bush Violet, but the only admissible dedicated page found for Browallia speciosa (NC State) leads its Common Name(s) list with Amethyst Flower and calls the plant 'The Amethyst Flower' in its description, naming Bush Violet among the 'Other common names'. MoBot and RHS pages could not be located or read, so there was no second source to split on.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Browallia speciosa page, under its "Caution:" heading in the description, says: "The Amethyst Flower is toxic to cats and dogs if ingested. Symptoms of poisoning include excessive drooling, loss of appetite, vomiting, diarrhea, weakness, slow heart rate, and death sometimes may occur." The page's separate Problems field under Landscape also carries the tags "Problem for Cats" and "Problem for Dogs". The page has no Poison block, names no poisonous plant part, gives no severity rating, and carries no handling warning, so none are recorded. Family membership (Solanaceae) is not used as toxicity evidence.
unknowns: Only NC State (plants.ces.ncsu.edu) had a usable dedicated Browallia speciosa page. No MoBot or RHS page could be reached: MoBot's Plant Finder redirects to plantfinder.mobot.org, which failed TLS certificate verification in the sandbox, and RHS's search is script-rendered so no species page URL could be found. Searches of UF/IFAS, UMD, Penn State, Clemson and UGA turned up no Browallia speciosa page. Every non-null field therefore rests on one source.

common_name: Amethyst Flower was chosen because NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list leads with it and its description opens 'The Amethyst Flower is...'. No second source could be checked, so a split with the catalog brief's Bush Violet cannot be ruled out.
chill_damage_f null: NC State gives only 'winter hardy in zones 9-11' and USDA zones 9a-11b, which are hardiness ratings, not a damage-onset temperature.
Temperature, humidity, light in foot-candles and fertilizer fields are null: NC State gives no figures or schedule. It says only 'over-fertilizing will promote foliage at the expense of flowers'.

direct_sun_hours_max null: the species prose says only 'sunlight with afternoon shade'. NC State's Light field values carry generic category labels: 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)', which is a minimum, and 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)'. These are site-wide legend text, not species-specific maxima.

outdoor_sun_exposure: the structured Light field lists Full sun and Partial Shade. Partial Shade is mapped to part_shade. The prose 'sunlight with afternoon shade' and the tag '#partial shade tolerant' are consistent with this.
soil_base null: NC State lists the plant for containers, hanging baskets and houseplants as well as beds and borders, and states no potting mix or garden-bed requirement.

soil_drainage moderate: from NC State's Soil Drainage tag 'Good Drainage' paired with the prose 'evenly moist, well-drained soil'. No waterlogging or root-rot warning contradicts it. No source requires consistently wet soil, so moisture_retentive is not set.

water_regime null: 'evenly moist' appears only as a soil preference inside the cultivation sentence, not as a watering instruction or structured moisture field. NC State also says over-watering promotes foliage at the expense of flowers. No dry-down depth or interval is given.

Soil pH bounds null: NC State's pH tags are Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0). The acid band is open-ended, and the 8.0 top of the Neutral band cannot be checked against an RHS pH field, which could not be read. The prose says 'somewhat acidic pH'.

is_edible null: no admissible source addresses eating the plant. NC State's Ethnobotany field says only that it is used as a medicine in Colombia (chewing leaves for a toothache), which is not food use.

Size: NC State's Dimensions block gives Height 1 ft 0 in - 2 ft 0 in and Width 1 ft 0 in - 2 ft 0 in (12-24 in each). Its prose also says the plant 'generally spreads 1 foot, but it can sometimes spread up to 3 feet', which is wider than the structured width. Cultivar sizes (for example 'Blue Bells' 1-12 inches) are not the species' size.

NC State lists Plant Type as Annual and Herbaceous Perennial, and Life Cycle as Annual and Perennial. The prose says it is a tropical herbaceous perennial that is frequently grown as a warm-weather annual.
toxicity_detail: NC State's Caution paragraph names cats and dogs together. No poison part list, severity rating or handling warning is given anywhere on the page.

records.name_note: Sources split on which common name leads. NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list is alphabetized (Mountain Savory, Winter Savory), while its Description calls the plant Winter Savory, and RHS's plant profile leads with "winter savory" with "winter savoury" as an other common name. Winter Savory was chosen because RHS leads with it and NC State's own prose uses it; Mountain Savory is the alternate name. It is a perennial, distinct from the annual Summer Savory (Satureja hortensis), which NC State flags as "often confused with" this plant; no lifespan or hardiness was borrowed from S. hortensis.
unknowns: No Missouri Botanical Garden page for Satureja montana was found (plant finder searches for 'satureja montana' and 'satureja' returned nothing), and no other admissible source was located, so the record rests on NC State and RHS.
toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null: neither NC State (no poison section on the page) nor RHS addresses toxicity to cats or dogs.
is_houseplant=false rests only on NC State's Plant Type field (Edible, Herb, Herbaceous Perennial) listing no houseplant value; no source frames it as a houseplant.

soil_drainage=fast is read from the NC State Description: it is easy to grow in 'sandy, well-drained soil' and 'does not do well in damp soil'. NC State's structured drainage tags are only Good Drainage and Occasionally Dry, with Soil Texture Sand and Shallow Rocky; RHS says only 'Well-drained'. No source says the soil must be sharp, so the fast reading is the borderline call.

water_regime is null: NC State states 'dry or medium levels of moisture' as a growing-condition adjective, not a watering instruction, and RHS gives only a bare 'Well-drained' moisture value. water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm and the day-interval fields are null because this is an in-ground perennial herb with no source framing watering that way.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0) bands, two of them open-ended, and RHS lists 'Alkaline or Neutral', so no closed floor or ceiling is supported.

direct_sun_hours_max is null: the only hour figure is NC State's site-wide light legend ('6 or more hours'), which is a minimum and not a species-specific maximum. The Description says the plant 'does tolerate light shade', which is a tolerance aside and was not added to outdoor_sun_exposure.

RHS's Cultivation line ('Grow in moderately fertile well-drained, preferably alkaline soil, in full sun') is genus boilerplate that also appears on the Satureja hortensis page, so it was not used for any field.

chill_damage_f is null: NC State gives only USDA zones 5a-10b and RHS only a UK H5 rating, which are survival ratings and not a damage-onset temperature. Other climate fields, humidity, fertilizer and light_fc are null for lack of admissible species evidence.

Edibility: NC State's Edibility field says 'Leaves can be used fresh or dried as a seasoning in food.' and its Description says the flowers are edible (spicy, peppery) and the leaves flavor meat, fish, salads, soup, stew and sausage. No source states any condition or hazard, and no other part is addressed. RHS lists the plant under Herbs - Culinary.

Size is NC State's Dimensions block (Height 0 ft 6 in to 1 ft 6 in = 6-18 in; Width 1 ft 0 in to 1 ft 6 in = 12-18 in). RHS gives Max Height and Max Spread of 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in) and 'up to 40cm tall and 20cm wide'; NC State was used as the anchor.
attracts_pollinators: NC State's Attracts field lists Butterflies only, while its Description says the flowers are very attractive to bees.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on which common name leads. NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list is alphabetized (Downy Cherry, Nanking Cherry) and its prose calls the plant Downy Cherry. RHS's plant profile renders Nanking cherry as the common name beneath the botanical name heading and lists downy cherry under "Other common names". Nanking Cherry was chosen as common_name because RHS singles it out as the main name; both names are recorded here.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page for Prunus tomentosa has no Poison block, no symptom list, no stated poisonous parts and no statement about leaves, stems or pits (no cyanogenic glycoside statement for this taxon). Its Problems field lists Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs and Problem for Horses, and its full tag run reads "#edible fruits #deciduous shrub #deciduous #naturalizes #showy fruits #drought tolerant #low maintenance #windbreak #erosion control #mass planting #food source soft mast fruit #food source fall #problem for dogs #problem for horses #problem for cats #eastern tiger swallowtail butterfly #butterfly friendly #larval host plant #pollinator plant #hedge #wildlife friendly #heat intolerant #cold tolerant #shrub border #screen". These are NC State's own tags, with no severity rating or symptoms attached. Plant Type is listed as Edible and Shrub, and Fruit Value To Gardener lists Edible and Showy. Edibility there reads: "Fruits are edible and range from tart to sweet. Use them in jams, jellies, pies and tarts." No cooking or ripeness condition is given, and nothing is said about eating other parts. RHS says the fruit is "edible but sharp" and says nothing about toxicity. The cat and dog tags therefore sit beside an edible-fruit plant: the edible statement covers the fruit only, the problem tags name no part, and the edible fruit should not be read as a statement that the rest of the plant is safe to eat.
unknowns: Missouri Botanical Garden (www.missouribotanicalgarden.org and plantfinder.mobot.org) was unreachable from the sandbox, so no MoBot content was used.
Clemson, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD and UGA searches returned no dedicated page for Prunus tomentosa, only genus-level or multi-species pages, which were not used.

toxic_to_pets rests only on NC State's Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags. No admissible source gives symptoms, severity, poisonous parts, or any cyanogenic glycoside or pit statement for this taxon.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), and the acid band is open-ended. RHS lists pH as Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, so alkaline soil is acceptable and no ceiling can be set.
water_regime is null: no watering statement was found. NC State has only the soil tag Moist and a drought-tolerance trait, neither of which is a watering instruction.

RHS gives Max Height 1.5-2.5 metres (59-98 in) and Max Spread 1.5-2.5 metres (59-98 in), smaller than NC State's 6-10 ft height and 6-15 ft width. Both are species pages. NC State's figures were used and RHS's smaller range is recorded here as a disagreement.

outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun only. NC State's Light field also lists 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)' and its prose says 'full sun to partial shade', but RHS's structured Position field renders 'Full sun' alone in both its summary card and its Growing Conditions block, so part_shade, resting on NC State alone, was dropped.
direct_sun_hours_max is null: the only hour figures come from NC State's generic light-category legend.
is_houseplant false: no admissible source addresses indoor culture; both pages treat it as an outdoor shrub. NC State's Plant Type field lists Edible and Shrub, and its USDA zones are 2a-7b.

Temperature, humidity, light in foot-candles, fertilizer, and chill damage are null: not stated by the admissible pages. NC State's zone 2a-7b range and its 'not recommended for sites south of USDA Zone 7' are hardiness and regional limits, not damage-onset temperatures.

is_edible true covers the fruits only (NC State: 'Fruits are edible and range from tart to sweet. Use them in jams, jellies, pies and tarts.'; RHS: 'edible but sharp'). Neither page names a poisonous part or says anything about the pits, so no part-level toxicity is recorded; the cat and dog problem tags are not tied to a part.

records.name_note: The common name 'Cleyera' is also the genus name of the separate species Cleyera japonica. NC State says Japanese ternstroemia or false Japanese cleyera is very similar and often mistakenly sold as Cleyera japonica, and its 'often confused with' module lists Cleyera japonica. NC State's Common Name(s) list (alphabetized) begins with Cleyera, though its Description opens with 'Japanese ternstroemia'. UF/IFAS's page title and Common name(s) line lead with Cleyera, so it is used as the primary name.
unknowns: No toxicity, pet-safety or edibility statement was found on the NC State or UF/IFAS pages for Ternstroemia gymnanthera, so toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail and is_edible are null; nothing was inferred from the tea family.

No RHS page for Ternstroemia gymnanthera could be located (the guessed RHS URLs returned 404). The only Missouri Botanical Garden page found was for the cultivar 'Carolina Sunset', which is cultivar-only and not used. So only NC State and UF/IFAS contributed.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State's Acid (<6.0) band is open-ended, its Neutral (6.0-8.0) ceiling cannot be checked against RHS's pH field, and UF/IFAS lists slightly alkaline among soil tolerances.

water_regime is null: both sources give only soil adjectives (NC State 'moist and well-drained', UF/IFAS 'moisture-retentive but well-drained'), not a watering statement. Dry-down, day-interval and fertilizer fields are null for an in-ground shrub with no such framing.

Size conflict: NC State gives Height 8 ft. 0 in. - 10 ft. 0 in. and Width 5 ft. 0 in. - 6 ft. 0 in. (used, converted to 96-120 and 60-72 inches); UF/IFAS gives Height 12 to 20 feet and Spread 5 to 10 feet.

Light: NC State's structured Light field lists full sun and partial shade (2-6 hours), but its prose says it does best in part shade and warns 'Winter burn may occur in full sun.' and 'Winter leaf scorching can occur in full sun.' UF/IFAS's structured Light requirement is 'plant grows in the shade' and its prose says only 'tolerant of full sun but grows best in partial shade'. full_sun was therefore dropped and part_shade kept. direct_sun_hours_max is null because no species-specific hour figure was found.
soil_base garden_bed is an in-ground landscape classification based on both sources treating this as a landscape shrub; neither names a potting mix.
No Attracts or pollinator statement was found on the NC State or UF/IFAS pages, so attracts_pollinators is null.

No source gave a cold-damage onset temperature; the zone ranges (NC State 7a-9b, UF/IFAS 7 through 10) are survival ratings and were not used for chill_damage_f. Temperature and humidity fields are null (outdoor shrub, no source).

is_houseplant false: no admissible source frames it as a houseplant. NC State's Plant Type field lists Perennial and Shrub and its USDA zones are 7a-9b; UF/IFAS treats it as a landscape plant for zones 7 through 10.

normalizations: 2026-10-09: b124 landed (mixed gaps: Bloodleaf, Statice, Cranberry Hibiscus, Amethyst Flower, Winter Savory, Cushaw Squash, Nanking Cherry, Cleyera). Auditor-supplied corrected wording used verbatim where it held; every added or changed quote ground-truthed with b124_qcheck.py (qc.py plus strict-node and rendered-body tests). Landing decisions: Alternanthera ficoidea lands as Bloodleaf, the first item of NC State's rendered alphabetized Common Name(s) list, not the requested Calico Plant (second item), because the Description's prose lead "Joseph's coat" is Amaranthus tricolor's landed name (b13); Limonium sinuatum stays Statice, the opener of NC State's Description, with Sea Lavender disclosed; every <title>-only NC State common-name parenthetical in the batch (Bloodleaf, Statice, Cranberry Hibiscus, Amethyst Flower, Winter Savory, Cushaw Squash, Nanking Cherry, Cleyera) re-quoted as the rendered stacked Common Name(s) list; RHS name claims re-quoted to the rendered plant-profile common name, with the RHS page title kept only beside a CORR Name Status citation; NC State label+value quotes trimmed to values; Nanking Cherry drops part_shade (RHS Position is Full sun alone) and Cleyera drops full_sun (two NC State scorch warnings, UF/IFAS Light requirement 'plant grows in the shade'); Nanking Cherry's toxicity_detail carries the full 25-tag run and names the fruit as the only edible part, with no poisonous part or pit statement on either page; Cushaw Squash's toxicity_detail restored from the auditor's wording (explicit #non-toxic for cats/dogs tags; edible fruits, seeds and flowers); Statice, Nanking Cherry and Cleyera is_houseplant null -> false, cited to Plant Type and USDA zone fields. No MoBot citation added.
